abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.

abstract: Conventional non-amplifying messenger RNA (mRNA) and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) medicines generally share a core linear RNA architecture-including a 5' cap, untranslated regions, one or more open reading frames, and a poly(A) tail-and are commonly formulated with delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to enable transient intracellular expression of a target protein. Prophylactic mRNA vaccines are designed primarily to express infectious-disease antigens and generate protective immune memory, whereas mRNA therapeutics exert pharmacological effects intended to treat disease, suppress recurrence, replace proteins, modulate immunity, or deliver gene-editing enzymes. Thus, even products based on similar mRNA-LNP technology may have different regulatory classifications and evidence requirements according to their intended use and mechanism of action. The clinical and regulatory landscape has expanded beyond the first coronavirus disease 2019 vaccines to include respiratory syncytial virus and influenza mRNA vaccines, an influenza-coronavirus disease 2019 combination vaccine, an authorized saRNA vaccine, personalized cancer immunotherapies, protein-replacement therapies, in vivo cell programming, and gene-editing delivery systems. This review examines which prophylactic-vaccine evidence can support therapeutic development and where product-specific quality, nonclinical, clinical, and lifecycle evidence remains necessary. For prophylactic mRNA vaccines, major regulatory considerations include quality, immunogenicity, preventive efficacy, lot release, and safety surveillance after large-scale vaccination. For mRNA therapeutics, the principal issues include delivery to target tissues, function of the expressed product, repeat-dose safety, biodistribution, off-target risk, long-term follow-up, and patient-specific manufacture and traceability. In particular, although personalized mRNA cancer vaccines are commonly described as vaccines, they are closer in regulatory purpose to therapeutics that act on the basis of each patient's tumor characteristics than to vaccines that prevent infectious disease. Antigen-selection algorithms, patient-specific sequence design, small-batch and multi-product manufacture, product-patient matching, clinical evaluation of combination strategies, manufacturing delays and analysis populations, and risk-based long-term postauthorization follow-up therefore require explicit regulatory consideration. Platform-level knowledge from prophylactic mRNA vaccine authorization can support therapeutic development, but regulatory questions may vary with each new product type; developers will need to track evolving regulatory instruments across jurisdictions and engage regulatory authorities early.

abstract: This is a phase IIb/III, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled, multi-centre, non-inferiority clinical trial that aims to determine safety, tolerability and immunogenicity of a booster vaccination with a recombinant protein receptor binding domain (RBD) fusion homodimer of XBB.1.16 adapted candidate against SARS-CoV-2 developed by HIPRA (PHH-1V81).
description:
This is a phase IIb/III, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled, multi-centre, non-inferiority clinical trial that aims to determine safety, tolerability and immunogenicity of a booster vaccination with a recombinant protein receptor binding domain (RBD) fusion homodimer of XBB.1.16 adapted candidate against SARS-CoV-2 developed by HIPRA (PHH-1V81).

Approximately 612 participants who have received a primary scheme with an EU-approved mRNA vaccine (two doses) and at least one booster dose of an EU-approved mRNA vaccine against COVID-19, will be randomly assigned to the following two treatment arms in a PHH-1V81 : Comirnaty (Omicron XBB.1.5) 2:1 ratio:

* PHH-1V81 vaccine arm: Approximately 408 adults will receive a booster dose of PHH-1V81 (HIPRA adapted vaccine).
* Comirnaty vaccine arm: Approximately 204 adults will receive a booster dose of Comirnaty Omicron XBB.1.5.

Participants will be stratified before randomisation by age group (approximately 10% of adults ≥60 years old), and by number of doses previously received.

All participants will receive a booster dose of PHH-1V81 or Comirnaty Omicron XBB.1.5 at Day 0 and will be followed for 6 months. All subjects will be closely observed for 15 minutes after vaccination on site.

abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.

abstract: Helper lipids are essential structural components of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), yet systematic design principles linking helper lipid architecture to messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery performance remain poorly defined. Here we identify helper lipid architecture as a major, largely unexplored design lever for optimizing LNP performance. Using a modular library of more than 80 rationally designed helper lipids, we show that systematic variation in headgroup chemistry, linker topology, and tail cardinality reshapes both LNP biophysical behavior and biological performance. Martini molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with multimodal structural analyses reveal that high-performing scaffolds undergo a pH-dependent transition into fusogenic inverse hexagonal-like ordering, substantially lowering the energetic barrier for endosomal escape. These performance gains persist across the clinically relevant ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA platforms, establishing helper lipid architecture as a transferable design parameter across distinct ionizable lipid chemistries. Translating these design principles into function, optimized helper lipid formulations restore hepatic protein expression in a mouse model of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency and increase antigen expression and immunogenicity in both preclinical models and in the in vitro human MIMIC platform. Together, these findings establish helper lipids as tunable molecular actuators of potency, tolerability, and stability, offering an engineering framework for next-generation mRNA vaccines and therapeutics.

abstract: RNA modifications are being investigated as contributors to multiple myeloma (MM) biology alongside genomic lesions and bone marrow interactions. This narrative review examines N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A), 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C), adenosine-to-inosine editing, and pseudouridylation, with emphasis on the distinction between MM-specific findings and mechanisms proposed from other systems. Functional studies in MM cells and animal models link METTL3, WTAP, FTO, ALKBH5, and YTHDF2 to selected growth, metabolic, and treatment-response programs. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has been implicated in GLI1 editing and regulation of double-stranded RNA sensing during lenalidomide exposure. Patient expression and outcome associations support clinical relevance but do not establish that these regulators determine disease behavior. Evidence for m⁵C is more limited, including an NSUN2-exosomal MALAT1 mechanism in myeloma bone disease, while the pseudouridylation studies discussed here largely concern non-myeloma cancers. Stage-specific regulatory changes across precursor disease and relapse remain hypotheses requiring longitudinal testing. Therapeutic approaches include enzyme inhibition, targeted protein degradation, and RNA-directed strategies; most remain preclinical, and several have been evaluated mainly outside MM. Plasma cell-free RNA studies provide early diagnostic observations, but modification-aware liquid biopsy has not been clinically validated for MM risk stratification, treatment selection, or relapse prediction. Progress will depend on disease-specific target validation, selective delivery, assessment of normal hematopoietic effects, and prospective clinical studies. Epitranscriptomic regulation therefore offers a useful research framework for understanding and potentially targeting MM, without displacing the established contribution of genomic and clinical risk factors.

title: Epitranscriptomic regulation contributes to multiple myeloma biology and offers potential therapeutic targets.

abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.

abstract: Targeted protein degradation has shown powerful capability for diseases treatment. However, the approach is limited by the challenges in cellular internalization of synthetic degrader and potential cytotoxicity. Herein, we propose a Genetically encoded circular RNA Aptamer-based DEgrader (GRADE) to control target proteins degradation. The GRADE system is facilely constructed by integrating a transferrin receptor (TfR1) aptamer and target protein aptamer for delivering target protein into damaged endosomes and TfR1 binding, leading to target protein degradation via endosomal autophagy pathways. We show that the versatile and modular GRADE could be applied to eliminate several intracellular target proteins. Moreover, the GRADE system can be selectively activated by endogenous biomarkers for achieving highly specific protein degradation and cancer cell precise inhibition. This study presents a non-invasive, effective and general platform for intracellular protein degradation, offering new insights into controlled cell manipulation and diseases therapy.

title: Genetically Encoded Engineering Switchable Circular RNA Devices for Targeted Protein Degradation.

abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

title: AI-guided CRISPR gene editing for cardiovascular disease: Current progress, transitional challenges, and future directions.

abstract: Here, we present a CRISPR-Cas9 protocol for generating both small indels and multi-kilobase deletions to enable genome editing in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We describe steps for a ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based approach that integrates guide RNA selection, electroporation, and multi-tiered screening to accurately identify indels, deletions, inversions, and mixed genotypes. Human iPSCs provide a versatile genome editing platform due to their capacity for clonal expansion and differentiation. This protocol provides a scalable framework for genome editing and quality control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Hamerlinck et al.1.

title: CRISPR-based pipeline for generating and validating multi-kb deletions and indels in iPSCs.

abstract: Identifying genes associated with the mechanism of action (MOA) of anticancer therapies is essential for understanding drug response. Functional genomics approaches, including genome-wide CRISPR knock out screens, enable systematic gene prioritization following treatment; however, findings from individual datasets are typically interpreted after identifying overlapping genes across datasets to confirm biological hypotheses. Integrating such heterogeneous datasets remains challenging due to variability across experimental conditions. Existing approaches can miss biologically relevant genes due to dataset-specific noise, can fail to capture genes exhibiting consistent but moderate effects across studies. Here, we present ConcuRx, a statistical framework for cross-study integration and gene prioritization across heterogeneous CRISPR drug-response screens. This approach produces more stable gene rankings than single-dataset analyses, improving prioritization of known MOA-associated genes and recovering biologically relevant genes that are overlooked by average- and overlap-based approaches. Applied to CRISPR drug-response screens for the synergistic drug pair of ATR and PARP inhibitors, ConcuRx strengthened support for 15 experimentally validated hypotheses collected from published studies, including mechanisms supported by independent studies not included in the ConcuRx analysis. These findings demonstrate that modelling between-study variability improves identification and prioritization of MOA-associated genes and provides a robust strategy for integrating heterogeneous functional genomics data in precision oncology.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Loss of function mutations in the lipid transporter ABCA7 have been linked to increased risk for late onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although rare and common variants in ABCA7 associated with AD alter the coding sequence and are predicted to impair protein function, the precise cell-type consequences of ABCA7 deficiency remain incompletely defined.
METHODS: We used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that were deficient for ABCA7 (ABCA7-KO) and their wild-type (ABCA7-WT) isogenic counterparts and subsequently performed unbiased proteomics on differentiated astrocytes (iAs), neurons (iNs) and microglia (iMGs). ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs produced the largest proteomic changes, so we therefore conducted additional functional analyses to define its effects on microglial lysosomal activity, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. In addition, we leveraged CRISPR/Cas9 to correct the ABCA7 rs3752246 AD risk variant in patient-derived iPSCs and compared proteomic and functional phenotypes between corrected iMGs and isogenic mutant carriers. Finally, we examined the functional consequence of ABCA7-deficient microglia on neurons.
RESULTS: ABCA7-KO iMGs were deficient for proteins involved in lysosome function, measured by down-regulated lysosomal proteomic signatures, as well as reduced DQ-BSA activity and reduced LAMP1+ area. Additionally, ABCA7-KO iMGs displayed impaired phagocytic capacity and increased inflammatory markers, including MHC proteins CD1A and CD1E, and IL-18,. Multi-omic integration of lipidomic and proteomic profiles nominated a dysregulated metabolic network characterized by altered phospholipid steady-state metabolism and increased lipid peroxidation in ABCA7-KO iMGs. This was complemented by an accumulation of polyunsaturated triacylglycerols and lipid droplets, suggesting that ABCA7 deficiency disrupts intracellular lipid dynamics. This was supported by the alleviation of lysosomal and lipid droplet phenotypes through the inhibiting the synthesis of triacylglycerols. Concordantly, proteomic and functional analyses revealed lysosomal dysfunction in rs3752246-mutant iMGs, suggesting a shared ABCA7-dependent mechanism underlying AD risk. Tri-cultures of iNs, iAs and iMGs revealed that ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs worsened AD-relevant neuronal measures such as tau phosphorylation and synapse number.
CONCLUSIONS: This work supplies evidence for the important role of ABCA7 in microglia and provides unique insights into the molecular and functional consequences of reduced ABCA7 function in lysosomal and lipid regulation, paving a path forward to a more comprehensive understanding of AD molecular subtypes and personalized therapeutics.

abstract: Adenoviral vectors have been widely validated as effective vaccine platforms for both infectious diseases and cancer due to their strong immunostimulatory properties. However, their application to personalized cancer vaccines and other time-sensitive antigens is limited by the prolonged production time required for conventional vector generation. Here, we developed an adenovirus-derived virus-like particle (Ad5VLP) platform that enables modular incorporation of antigen cargo without reconstruction of a complete antigen-encoding adenoviral genome. Ad5VLPs successfully packaged and delivered foreign mRNA, although mRNA-derived antigen expression remained insufficient to induce robust antigen-specific immunity in vivo. In contrast, direct encapsulation of protein or peptide antigens substantially improved intracellular antigen delivery and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigen presentation. Following subcutaneous prime-boost immunization in mice, antigen-loaded Ad5VLPs induced robust antigen-specific interferon-γ (IFN-γ) responses, with functional activity preferentially enriched within CD44hi CD8+ T cells and accompanied by effector-associated CD8+ T-cell differentiation. Importantly, robust cellular immune responses were also observed using an E0771 tumor neoantigen, demonstrating that the platform extends beyond the model ovalbumin (OVA) antigen. Protein-loaded Ad5VLPs also elicited antigen-specific and antivector humoral responses. Vaccination was well tolerated over the 14 day study period, with no substantial changes in body weight, clinical observations, serum markers of hepatic or renal injury and systemic inflammation, or broad splenic inflammatory transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings demonstrate that Ad5VLPs enable modular delivery of protein and peptide antigens and induce robust cellular immune responses, supporting further investigation for personalized cancer vaccination and other time-sensitive vaccine applications.

abstract: C9ORF72 is involved in multiple neuronal functions and a major factor in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, a fatal neurodegenerative disease. Pathogenicity is implemented through an intronic repeat expansion in the gene's mRNA leader that produces long, repetitive RNA and dipeptides when translated through repeat associated non-canonical translation. The expanded repeat also suppresses transcription of the major transcript variant (Variant 2) which comprises 90% of the C9ORF72 levels in healthy cells, leading to an additional loss-of-function effect. Examining the sequence, structure, and ribosome occupancy of Variant 2's mRNA leader in detail, we found that translation of C9ORF72 is tightly regulated through a multi-layered system. To deconvolute this system, we conducted a mutant screen and developed a method to evaluate the results quantitatively. We found that near-cognate start codons in all three frames, a start-stop element in frame 2, a uTranslon in frame 1, and secondary structures cooperate to keep baseline C9ORF72 translation low. Further, initiation at upstream near-cognate start codons reduces the impact of both the start-stop and the uTranslon, effectively buffering their repressive function and creating a feedforward loop. A strong secondary structure in the Variant 2-specific sequence further modulates initiation at all the elements. We hypothesize that this buffered repressor system has evolved to ensure reliable, noise-insensitive expression of this critical regulator of neuronal function. Finally, we used ADAR-based RNA editing of specific sites in Variant 2's mRNA leader, increasing translation of the gene and providing a novel avenue to rescue the loss-of-function phenotype in disease.

abstract:
The global objective of this Basket of Basket study is to evaluate the antitumor activity of each matched therapies that will be evaluated through the study in small molecularly selected populations.

The objective of module 1 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 12 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of atezolizumab in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive atezolizumab 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks.

The objective of module 2 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 16 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of futibatinib in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive will receive futibatinib, 20 mg, once daily (QD) in 28-day cycles.

The objective of module 3 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 12 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of amivantamab in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive amivantamab 1050 mg intravenously (IV) for body weight \< 80 kg and 1400 mg for body weight \>= 80 kg mg once weekly in Cycle 1 (with a split dose on Days 1-2) and then every 2 weeks in subsequent cycles (28-day cycles).

description:
Basket studies are a new sort of clinical studies to identify patients with the same kind of mutations and treat them with the same drug, irrespective of their specific cancer type. In basket studies, depending on the mutation types, patients are classified into "baskets". Targeted therapies that block that mutation are then identified and assigned to baskets where patients are treated accordingly.

This protocol has two parts: part A (iPROFILER), which includes the common procedures for tumor molecular profiling and treatment recommendation, and part B (iBASKET), which corresponds to the therapeutic portion.

The purpose of part A (iPROFILER) of this study is to test participants' tumour tissue in order to identify whether their tumour has certain mutations in cancer-related genes. It is known that gene mutations of tumours contribute to their origin and growth and determine whether the tumour will respond to particular cancer drugs. This test will provide information about potential targeted therapies that specifically attack those gene mutations. The purpose of part B (iBASKET) of this study is to offer participants a personalised anti-cancer treatment based on the gene mutations that are found in their tumour.

Participants taking part in module 1 of part B (iBASKET) will receive atezolizumab 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks, following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take atezolizumab for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 1 will have a 2-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, atezolizumab. Approximately 1000 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 120 participants being recruited into module 1 of part B (iBASKET).

Participants taking part in module 2 of part B (iBASKET) will receive will receive futibatinib, 20 mg, once daily (QD) in 28-day cycles, following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take futibatinib for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 2 will have a 2-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, futibatinib. Approximately 1000 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 80 participants being recruited into module 2 of part B (iBASKET).

Participants taking part in module 3 of part B (iBASKET) will receive amivantamab 1050 mg IV for body weight \< 80 kg and 1400 mg for body weight \>= 80 kg mg once weekly in Cycle 1 (with a split dose on Days 1-2) and then every 2 weeks in subsequent cycles (28-day cycles), following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take amivantamab for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 3 will have a 2.5-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, amivantamab. Approximately 1725 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 69 participants being recruited into module 3 of part B (iBASKET).

abstract: The purpose of this study is to determine whether carnosine (a food ingredient found in chicken and red meat) supplementation (2 g) for 6 months in participants with non-claudication and claudication peripheral arterial disease (PAD) improves walking ability. Previous studies with heart failure patients have shown that carnosine supplementation increases walking capacity in these patients.

description: The objective of this double-blinded longitudinal study is to determine whether carnosine supplementation (2 g) for 6 months in participants with non-claudication and claudication peripheral arterial disease (PAD) improves walking ability. In this pilot study we will enroll 144 participants that will be divided into placebo (n=60) and carnosine groups (n=60). We will measure the distance covered on the 6-minute walk test (6-MWT) and the pain free walking capacity on the treadmill before and after the placebo or carnosine supplementation. We will measure ankle branchial index (ABI) and blood flow by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before and after the carnosine and placebo supplementation. In addition, we will measure carnosine by 1HMRS (Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy), perform, global metabolomics and proteomics in the skeletal muscle, a comprehensive lipid and metabolic profile of blood, uptake of carnosine in red blood cells (RBCs), and measure carnosine aldehyde conjugates in the urine before and after 6 months of carnosine and placebo supplementation. Following completion of the study, we will follow the participants for another 3 months and examine the durability of carnosine supplementation.

abstract: Existing nucleoside analogues (NAs) and interferon therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) have limitations, including drug resistance, low HBsAg clearance rates, and irreversible immunosuppression. Therapeutic vaccines, by activating virus-specific T cells and B cells, hold promise for achieving functional cure (HBsAg clearance + sustained HBV DNA negativity). This study is an open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation Phase I clinical trial. The study population consists of patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection who have achieved virological stability following standard antiviral therapy. Phase I (dose exploration): three dose groups, with three patients per group. The primary objective is to observe and evaluate the safety of the WGc0201 vaccine in the study population (incidence and severity of adverse events).

institutions.label: West China Hospital

description: Although current antiviral treatments have achieved some clinical efficacy, there is still a lack of treatments that can truly cure hepatitis B, especially those that can completely eliminate HBsAg and prevent viral recurrence. Therapeutic hepatitis B vaccines are considered a potential treatment option for chronic hepatitis B and drug-resistant hepatitis B patients in the future. The development goal of therapeutic vaccines is to activate the body's specific immune response, promote the immune system to recognize and eliminate the hepatitis B virus, thereby achieving virological clearance and functional cure. WGc-0201 injection is an mRNA vaccine encoding the HBV-positive tumor antigen HBx. Preliminary basic research conducted by the team suggests that this vaccine has excellent safety, not only effectively clearing HBV DNA but also reducing HBsAg levels in serum and liver tissue while enhancing the expansion of specific T lymphocytes in the body. Therefore, we believe that the efficacy and safety of WGc0201 in treating hepatitis B warrant further investigation. We aim to use this Phase I study to preliminarily explore the therapeutic efficacy and safety of WGc0201 in this population and lay the groundwork for future clinical trials.

abstract:
This is an open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, recommended subsequent dose, pharmacokinetic profile, and preliminary efficacy of JCXH-213 in adult patients with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) who are refractory or relapsed after treatment with corticosteroids and second-line therapies.

The study consists of a screening period, treatment period, end-of-treatment visit, safety follow-up, and study withdrawal visit. Two dose groups are planned: 2 mg and 4 mg, with 2 patients to be enrolled in each dose group. During the treatment period, JCXH-213 at the assigned dose will be administered once every other day for a total of 7 doses. Assessments for safety and efficacy will be conducted according to the study schedule. After the last dose, patients will undergo an end-of-treatment visit and safety follow-up until the end of the study.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Trypanosoma cruzi, the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, alternates between replicative epimastigotes and amastigotes and non-dividing, mammal-infective metacyclic and bloodstream trypomastigotes. Protein phosphorylation is a major regulatory mechanism in trypanosomatids, whose kinomes reveal an expanded family of NIMA-related kinases (NEKs). Here, we investigated the role of T. cruzi RDK2 (repressor of differentiation kinase 2), a conserved NEK that carries a C-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. Endogenous gene tagging showed that TcRDK2 is expressed in all major life cycle stages and displays a cytoplasmic distribution. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TcRDK2 did not markedly alter epimastigote growth in rich medium but caused a significant accumulation of cells with abnormal nucleus/kinetoplast configurations, consistent with defects in kinetoplast segregation and cytokinesis; TcRDK2-null parasites also showed reduced in vitro metacyclogenesis and failed to establish efficient infections in human fibroblasts. To probe gain-of-function effects, we generated tetracycline-inducible overexpression lines for full-length TcRDK2 (RDK2WT), a PH-deleted variant (RDK2ΔPH), and a catalytically dead mutant (RDK2K70A). Overexpression of RDK2WT or RDK2ΔPH decreased epimastigote growth, enhanced metacyclogenesis, and strongly impaired host cell invasion and intracellular amastigote proliferation, with more pronounced phenotypes for RDK2ΔPH, suggesting that the PH domain normally restrains TcRDK2 activity in vivo. Phosphoproteomic profiling of RDK2WT-overexpressing epimastigotes revealed broad phosphoproteome remodeling associated with TcRDK2 upregulation, including changes affecting proteins linked to translation initiation and the cytoskeleton. Together, these findings support a role for TcRDK2 as a NEK kinase in kinetoplast replication/segregation, metacyclogenesis, and host cell infection in T. cruzi and highlight TcRDK2 as a promising kinetoplastid-specific therapeutic target for Chagas disease.
IMPORTANCE: Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major health problem with limited treatment options. To persist in both insect vectors and mammalian hosts, the parasite must precisely coordinate cell division, differentiation into infectious forms, and survival inside host cells. Protein kinases are central regulators of these processes and attractive drug targets, yet many remain poorly understood in T. cruzi. In this study, we investigate RDK2, a member of the NIMA-related kinase family. Using gene knockout, inducible overexpression, and global analysis of phosphorylated proteins, we show that RDK2 is required for accurate segregation of mitochondrial DNA, efficient formation of infective insect stage forms, and successful infection and replication in human cells. These findings identify RDK2 as a key regulator that links parasite cell division to infectivity and highlight it as a promising, parasite-specific candidate for future drug development against Chagas disease.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Cervical cancer can progress from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions driven by persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Identifying the gatekeepers restraining malignant transformation could reveal strategies to prevent and treat cervical cancer. In this study, we integrated single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 screening, and organoid modeling to dissect this process. Single-cell analysis of patient samples revealed progressive activation of rat sarcoma virus (RAS) and proliferation programs along epithelial differentiation paths. A focused CRISPR screen in HPV-positive pretumoroids identified neurofibromin 1 (NF1) as the top suppressor of malignant transition. NF1 loss accelerated carcinogenesis in organoids, substantially shortening the experimental interval required for the emergence of malignant phenotypes and recapitulating basal cell expansion, altered differentiation marker expression, and tumorigenicity. Mechanistically, NF1 loss enhanced RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B signaling, promoted proliferative programs, and remodeled chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions enriched for activator protein 1 motifs. Conversely, NF1 restoration in cancer organoids induced apoptosis and suppressed malignant maintenance. Artificial intelligence-guided modeling was used to design a minimal NF1-derived peptide predicted to interact with RAS GTP-binding protein. The NF1-GAP-mimetic peptide reduced tumor organoid viability and cervical lesion-associated bioluminescence in an HPV16-driven mouse model and was associated with local immune-related changes without marked alterations in selected splenic T-cell populations. Together, these findings establish NF1 as a critical constraint on HPV-associated epithelial evolution and provide a time-compressed organoid model of cervical carcinogenesis, offering proof of concept for NF1-inspired therapeutic interception of RAS-associated signaling.
SIGNIFICANCE: Single-cell atlas and organoid screening identified NF1 loss as a driver of cervical carcinogenesis, which can be rescued with an AI-designed NF1 mimetic peptide that offers a therapeutic paradigm to intercept tumorigenesis.

abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

abstract:
To evaluate whether individuals drawn from the intended use population can successfully interpret and follow the IFU for the Mia by XytoTest self-collection device and perform a vaginal sample collection yielding sufficient cellular material for primary hrHPV screening.

To assess the clinical performance of Mia self-collected vaginal specimens by evaluating agreement with paired clinician-collected cervical specimens for the detection of high-risk HPV, when both specimen types are analyzed using the cobas HPV Test (Roche Molecular Systems). Residual samples may be used to determine adequacy for additional assays that require vaginal and/or cervical specimens (such as mRNA E6 and E7 Biomarker Test, dual stain cytology).
description: The purpose of this pivotal study is to generate the clinical evidence necessary to support FDA marketing authorization for the Mia device. Specifically, the study will evaluate the diagnostic agreement of Mia-collected self-samples against the standard of care clinician-collected method for primary hrHPV detection, confirm device safety, demonstrate that end users across a diverse population can use the device safely and effectively as directed.

abstract:
Obesity is a complex, multifactorial disease driven by metabolic dysfunction, chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. The pathogenesis of obesity is closely linked to white adipose tissue (WAT) dysfunction, particularly the dysregulation of lipogenic and adipogenic pathways, leading to adipocyte hypertrophy and ectopic fat deposition. Although sleeve gastrectomy is a gold-standard intervention for severe obesity, a subset of patients experiences suboptimal long-term weight loss and cardiometabolic improvements, potentially due to persistent inflammation and metabolic resistance.

The gut-adipose axis has emerged as a critical therapeutic target. Modulation of the gut microbiome through synbiotic supplementation may alleviate metabolic endotoxemia and systemic inflammation, thereby improving energy homeostasis. However, the impact of presurgical synbiotic intervention on adipose tissue remodeling in patients undergoing sleeve gastrectomy remains largely unexplored.

This triple-blind, randomized controlled trial (RCT) aims to evaluate the efficacy of synbiotic supplementation in obese women candidates for sleeve gastrectomy. The objective is to investigate the effect of synbiotics on the expression of key lipogenic and adipogenic transcriptional factors (e.g., SREBP-1c, C/EBPα, PPARγ, LXRs) and rate-limiting enzymes (e.g, FAS, ACC) in white adipose tissue.

The study hypothesis is that presurgical synbiotic intervention will modulate adipose tissue function, thereby enhancing postoperative weight loss and improving metabolic profiles. The study aims to provide evidence for a potential therapeutic strategy to optimize clinical outcomes in bariatric patients by targeting the molecular mechanisms underlying adipose tissue expansion.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that causes dysregulation of keratinocyte proliferation, IL-23/IL-17-driven immune activation, oxidative stress and impaired barrier function. Biologics and targeted small molecules have improved clinical results, but systemic administration and lack of lesion specificity limit precise, long-term control of the disease. This paper revises the concept of psoriasis therapy from transdermal drug delivery to intelligent immune microenvironment reprogramming. Programmable biomaterial platforms that can actively recognize pathological signals and achieve spatiotemporal control of drug release, immune cell targeting, gene regulation and tissue remodelling have been introduced. Recently, there have been many developments in stimuli-responsive hydrogels, microneedle-based gene editing, biomimetic nanoplatforms, extracellular matrix-inspired scaffolds, and image-guided theranostic systems that link disease mechanisms, material design and therapeutic functions in a unified framework. We have further put forward the idea of cytokine blockade as a network-level immune recalibration, enhanced penetration and lesion-specific adaptive regulation, and image-guided precise intervention over empirical treatment. The three main translation problems are lesion heterogeneity, controllable immune modulation and large-scale manufacturing and long-term safety. This review provides a plan for developing intelligent, personalized biomaterial-based therapies for personalized psoriasis management.

abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a combination of motor, ocular, cognitive, and behavioural impairment, but has a heterogeneous clinical presentation. It is a devastating and rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian disorder with no current disease-modifying treatments. PSP is classified as a primary tauopathy characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau within neurons and glial cells, primarily in the brain stem, culminating in cell death. While genome wide association studies have been instrumental in identifying multiple risk loci, recent multi-omics studies combining brain gene expression and other omics measures have revealed a plethora of perturbed transcripts and molecular pathways that may play pivotal roles in PSP. This includes genes such as MAPT, STOM, KANK2, DDR2, LRRK2, and STX6, but their precise roles remain elusive. These genes are differentially expressed and may regulate processes including neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance of tau, cytoskeletal maintenance, and synaptic function. In this review, we summarise current treatment strategies attempted in PSP, compile disease-modifying therapies in development, and explore potential disease mechanisms suggested by multi-omics studies. By targeting several underlying disease processes at once, combination strategies have the potential to improve both motor and cognitive function, slow neurodegeneration, and ultimately alter disease progression.

abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a prevalent chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by genetic susceptibility, epidermal barrier dysfunction, and immune dysregulation. This review systematically expounds and analyzes the intricate cellular interactions between immune cells and keratinocytes (KCs) and their central roles in AD pathogenesis. The analysis emphasizes bidirectional crosstalk among diverse immune populations, such as Th2, Th17, regulatory T, and cytotoxic T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, mediated by cytokines, chemokines, and surface molecules, as well as how this cellular communication orchestrates key disease features, including inflammation, barrier breakdown, and chronic itch. Key signaling pathways, such as the JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and MAPK pathways, along with molecular targets including thymic stromal lymphopoietin, interleukin-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Rα), OX40/OX40 ligand, protease-activated receptor 2, transient receptor potential vanilloid channels, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor, are critically evaluated for their contributions to disease mechanisms. The review also surveys current and emerging therapeutic approaches, ranging from biologics targeting IL-4Rα/IL-13 and small-molecule inhibitors to combination regimens and novel strategies involving microbiome modulation and gene editing. Future investigations should advance personalized medicine paradigms to improve the long-term control and management of AD.

abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely on cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signaling to activate ancillary nucleases such as Csm6, which serve as core effectors in antiviral immunity. While cOA-mediated Csm6 activation has been widely harnessed for molecular diagnostics, its broader application is constrained by inherent limitations, including poor cellular permeability and susceptibility to degradation by ring nucleases. Here, we conducted a high-throughput fluorescence-based screen and identified DMPCH (7,8-dimethyl-4-phenylchroman-2-one) as a non-nucleotide allosteric activator of Thermus thermophilus (Tt) Csm6. DMPCH selectively stimulates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity by binding to the higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding domain dimerization interface, leading to expansion of the catalytic pocket and remodeling of the R-X4-6-H catalytic motif. Moreover, DMPCH acts synergistically with cA4 to activate TtCsm6, enabling rapid and sensitive RNA detection in a Cas13a-Csm6 system. Cell-based assays confirm that DMPCH activates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity in live bacteria cells. When combined with DMPCH, an engineered miniCsm6 fused to pyocin S2 (PyS2) exerts potent and specific bactericidal activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Our work establishes a framework for discovering non-nucleotide activators of CRISPR-associated ribonucleases and highlights their potential as chemical tools in cell-based research and as therapeutic agents against bacterial pathogens.

abstract: SMARCA4 (BRG1) is a critical ATPase subunit of canonical BAF complexes and a known long-term dependency in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS). To define the short-term consequences of SMARCA4 loss, we used a doxycycline-inducible shRNA system in Rh4 cells. Doxycycline treatment produced strong SMARCA4 knockdown, yet acute knockdown did not alter proliferation or induce myogenic differentiation. Ki-67 positivity remained unchanged, and Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) expression was absent, indicating preservation of the undifferentiated, proliferative ARMS phenotype. These findings contrast with CRISPR-mediated SMARCA4 knockout studies, which report cell-cycle exit and robust differentiation, suggesting that ARMS cells tolerate partial or early-phase SMARCA4 loss without destabilizing BAF complex function or PAX3-FOXO1-driven regulatory circuitry. Together with prior long-term knockdown studies, our results support a model in which SMARCA4 dependency in ARMS is a sustained phenomenon requiring deep, prolonged suppression to trigger differentiation and loss of tumor viability.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The use of tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against SOD1, has been recommended for the treatment of SOD1-ALS by current European guidelines. Before full approval by national health funding agencies, patients received tofersen through the Early Access Program (EAP) and/or as rescue therapy.
AIM OF THE STUDY: The aim of the study was to prospectively analyze clinical outcomes and neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentration in patients participating in the EAP in Poland between October 2023 and October 2025.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: Twenty patients with SOD1-ALS (11 with familial and 9 with sporadic ALS; male:female ratio, 2.2:1) were enrolled in the EAP. They carried 11 SOD1 pathological variants, the most frequent being L145S and K4E. As 1 patient withdrew after the first dose of treatment, data were collected from 19 individuals. The median age at disease onset was 49 years (33-69 years). Disease duration before treatment was 39 months (8-110 months), and the median age at initiation of tofersen treatment was 51 years (39-74 years). The analysis included demographic and genetic data, ALS functional rating scale-revised (ALSFRS- -R), ALS progression rate, forced vital capacity (FVC), adverse events, and NfL concentration in cerebrospinal fluid.
RESULTS: The median duration of tofersen treatment was 16 months (7-24 months). ALSFRS-R stabilized or increased in 68% of cases. Median delta ALSFRS-R during the treatment period was 0/month. The overall median progression rate decreased significantly from 0.218/month before treatment to 0.145/month at the last assessment (p < 0.0001). The decrease was observed in all patients, including fast-progressing individuals with continuous functional decline, as well as those with the most benign disease course. Two patients developed respiratory insufficiency, while FVC did not deteriorate in the remaining subjects. NfL concentration decreased in all analyzed patients, with significant reductions after 9 and 14 months. Serious treatment-related adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 3 patients and resolved without clinical consequences in 2 individuals. Two patients died due to disease progression and/or exacerbation of a preexisting condition/SAE.
CONCLUSIONS: The long-term follow-up data support the clinical efficacy and acceptable safety profile of tofersen treatment and demonstrate a biomarker response reflecting reduced axonal injury in both slow- and fast-progressing SOD1-ALS.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to diagnose early and treat effectively. The related microRNAs miR-221 and miR-222 share a seed sequence, but their functions and clinical evidence should be evaluated individually. Pancreatic cancer models support miR-221/222-associated TIMP-2 repression and invasion, miR-222-mediated p57 regulation, and tumor-derived vesicular miR-222 effects on p27 expression and localization. Macrophage-derived extracellular vesicular miR-222-3p has also been implicated in gemcitabine resistance through TSC1-associated signaling. By contrast, the TRPS1-ZEB2 mechanism and the vesicular SPINT1-HGF liver pathway derive from breast and colorectal cancer studies, respectively, and remain extrapolations when discussed in PDAC. Circulating miR-221 has shown exploratory diagnostic associations, but results from general miRNA panels cannot be assigned to miR-221 or miR-222 individually. Tissue prognostic associations likewise do not validate circulating assays. A first-in-human study of the selective inhibitor LNA-i-miR-221 provides early safety and peripheral-blood pharmacodynamic evidence in a mixed advanced-cancer population that included pancreatic cancer; it does not establish PDAC-specific efficacy. Translation requires independent biomarker validation, molecule-specific target-dependence studies, and confirmation of effective pancreatic tumor delivery.

title: miR-221 and miR-222 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: mechanistic evidence, extracellular vesicle communication, biomarker candidates, and therapeutic prospects.

abstract: RNA therapeutics are an exciting class of medications that target RNA and/or are themselves made from RNA. Most RNA therapeutics that have been approved for clinical use are antisense oligonucleotides or small interfering RNAs. To date, eight RNA therapeutics with cardiovascular relevance have received US Food and Drug Administration approval, but not all of them have specific indications for treating cardiovascular disease. There is a promising pipeline of additional cardiovascular RNA therapies targeting lipoprotein(a), angiopoietin-like protein 3, and angiotensinogen. Chemical modifications to therapeutic nucleic acids are important for conferring nuclease resistance and limiting immunostimulation in vivo, and enhanced delivery can be achieved using N-acetylgalactosamine conjugation and/or lipid nanoparticles. Emerging approaches include stereopure oligonucleotide chemistry, circular RNAs, adenosine-to-inosine RNA base editing, and nonhepatic targeting. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of each modality, the clinical evidence for approved cardiovascular RNA therapeutics, selected pipeline candidates in advanced trials, and directions for future development.

abstract: Targeted reduction of hepatic antithrombin (AT) via siRNA offers a promising strategy to enhance thrombin (TMB) generation in bleeding disorders, though efficient hepatocyte delivery remains challenging. This study developed and evaluated a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation incorporating a novel morpholine-based ionizable lipid (MIL) and a lactobionic-octadecylamine conjugate (LBN) for hepatocyte-specific delivery of AT-siRNA (siAT). Following synthesis of MIL and LBN, siAT-loaded LNP (siAT LNP LBN) were prepared using microfluidics and characterized for size, morphology, zeta potential, polydispersity index, and encapsulation efficiency (EE). Functional assays on HepG2 cells assessed cellular uptake, protein knockdown, and AT activity. The optimized formulation exhibited uniform particles (124 nm, PDI 0.125, zeta potential - 8.9 mV) and high EE (90%). Cytotoxicity assays confirmed safety up to 65 pmol siRNA. LBN-decorated LNP significantly enhanced hepatocyte uptake compared to non-targeted LNP and naked siRNA. Optimal AT mRNA suppression occurred at ~ 65 pmol siRNA and 16 h, with protein knockdown confirmed at 48 h. Functionally, siAT LNP LBN reduced AT activity to 48.1 ± 5.5%, substantially outperforming non-targeted LNP (64.1%) and naked siRNA (86.6%). The developed siAT-LNP-LBN platform demonstrated efficient hepatocyte uptake, robust AT knockdown, and low cytotoxicity in vitro, providing preliminary evidence for its potential as a hepatocyte-targeted siRNA delivery platform. Further in vivo studies are warranted to evaluate its biodistribution, liver-targeting efficiency, pharmacodynamic effects, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety.

abstract: Polysaccharide-centered engineering of biomass-derived nanoparticles (BNPs) is emerging as a sustainable and biologically compatible strategy for precision medicine. Polysaccharide-derived nanoparticles offer renewable sources, structural diversity, tunable physicochemical properties, and intrinsic biological functions that enable their rational engineering for targeted delivery and therapeutic modulation. This review focuses on cellulose-, chitosan-, alginate-, and hyaluronic acid-based nanoplatforms and examines how their molecular and supramolecular characteristics govern nanoparticle construction, nano-bio interactions, and therapeutic performance. Selected protein-derived systems are discussed where they form hybrid architectures with polysaccharides or provide mechanistic insights directly relevant to polysaccharide nanoengineering. We integrate bottom-up molecular assembly and top-down structural deconstruction as complementary fabrication paradigms and analyze how BNPs navigate physiological barriers through mechanisms including receptor-mediated transport, tight-junction modulation, and stimulus-responsive structural reconfiguration. We further examine their applications in CRISPR-Cas9 delivery and precision immunotherapy, with particular attention to design principles, translational constraints, and opportunities for scalable manufacturing. By linking molecular structure, assembly behavior, biological transport, and therapeutic function, this review provides a polysaccharide-centered framework for the rational development of adaptive biomass-derived nanoplatforms for precision medicine.

abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.

abstract: Rare genetic diseases affect over 350 million patients worldwide and have long posed significant challenges in modern medicine. Although messenger RNA (mRNA) was initially considered unsuitable due to its instability, immunogenicity, and inability to cross biological barriers, the COVID-19 pandemic established mRNA as a clinically validated therapeutic. Advances in mRNA synthesis and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) design have since improved stability, translation, safety, and scalability, offering a modern strategy, alongside advances in our understanding of rare diseases. By enabling the production of functional proteins without modifying the genome, mRNA-LNP offer a flexible solution to restore proteins lost through rare genetic diseases. Despite this promise, their application for rare genetic diseases remains at early stages, with most candidates in preclinical developments or early Phase 1/2 trials. This review underlines recent advances in mRNA-based protein replacement for rare genetic disorders, integrating innovations in mRNA design combined with LNPs optimization. It also discusses current challenges, emerging innovations, and future perspectives. While early clinical programs have mainly targeted liver-based disorders, the field is expanding toward pulmonary, hematologic, and neuromuscular diseases. Continued multidisciplinary efforts may establish mRNA nanotherapies as a transformative treatment option for patients with rare genetic disorders.

abstract: Excess lipid accumulation and a sedentary lifestyle are associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), but the causal mechanisms and preventive methods are not fully understood. Macroautophagy/autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway robustly induced by exercise and plays a key role in lipid metabolism. Understanding the mechanisms by which exercise activates autophagy and elicits metabolic benefits in the liver will provide important insights into the pathogenesis of MAFLD. Here, we discovered negative correlations between expression and lactylation of WDR41 (WD repeat domain 41) and pathogenesis of a series of human hepatic metabolic diseases. We found that WDR41 was a pro-autophagy protein that underwent lactylation in response to autophagy-inducing conditions, such as exercise. WDR41 was lactylated at lysine 319 (K319), a modification facilitated by LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A) upon autophagy induction, and delactylated by SIRT2 (sirtuin 2). Lactylated WDR41 promoted autophagy initiation by directly interacting with the autophagy proteins ATG13 (autophagy related 13) and RB1CC1/FIP200 (RB1 inducible coiled-coil 1) and driving the ULK1 (unc-51 like autophagy activating kinase 1) complex assembly. Physiologically, WDR41 and WDR41K319 lactylation, were important for exercise-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism against excess lipid accumulation in the liver. Thus, we demonstrated that WDR41 lactylation at K319 is an important regulatory mechanism by which exercise regulates autophagy and hepatic glucose and lipid metabolism.Abbreviations: AV: adeno-associated virus; title: Individualized antisense oligonucleotide therapy for SCN2A-related developmental epileptic encephalopathy beyond seizure control: A word of caution regarding the development of precision medicine neuropharmaceuticals.

abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

abstract: Saccharomyces boulardii (S. boulardii) is the only yeast probiotic widely used in clinical practice and consumer products. It combines gastrointestinal robustness, intrinsic antibiotic tolerance and eukaryotic protein-processing capacity, making it an attractive chassis for engineered probiotics, in situ biomanufacturing and live biotherapeutic delivery. However, host-specific characterization of regulatory elements, candidate genomic integration sites, and multicopy integration strategies remains limited in the clinically used S. boulardii CNCM I-745 background. Here, using S. boulardii CNCM I-745 as the host, we developed and characterized a genetic engineering toolkit that integrates transcriptional control elements with genome-integration strategies. We first quantified the activities of 20 endogenous constitutive promoters, two inducible promoters and six terminators. We then established a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow and evaluated 10 chromosomal integration loci; six of which showed Editing efficiency above 80% while supporting comparable transgene expression without detectable growth penalties. Finally, we constructed an rDNA-repeat-based multicopy integration system that increased transgene expression by 9.8- to 22.6-fold relative to single-copy integration and revealed a significant positive but non-proportional association between estimated copy number and reporter output. Together, this toolkit provides S. boulardii with a set of tunable promoters and terminators, candidate chromosomal integration sites compatible with a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow. These resources expand the genetic accessibility of this probiotic yeast and provide a foundation for developing engineered S. boulardii strains with enhanced probiotic, therapeutic and biomanufacturing functions.

abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing by ADAR1 is a key post-transcriptional modification, and mutations in ADAR1 lead to Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS), an autoimmune disorder. Despite its biological and clinical relevance, the regulation of ADAR1 activity remains incompletely understood. Using a combination of biochemical approaches, inositol-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (IPPK)-knockout cells, molecular dynamics simulations, and a cell-permeable inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) prodrug (Pro-IP6), we demonstrate that IP6 depletion drastically reduces global RNA editing, while supplementation with Pro-IP6 restores and even enhances editing levels. Furthermore, we identify the C6-phosphate of IP6 as a critical determinant of ADAR1 catalytic efficiency, functioning within a hydrogen-bonding network that indirectly coordinates a Zn2+-ion. Finally, we show that the AGS-associated ADAR1 mutation N907S impairs RNA editing activity, most likely by altering the hydrogen-bond interaction network linking IP6 to the ADAR1 catalytic center. Together, these findings identify IP6 as an essential cofactor and regulator of ADAR1 activity and highlight cofactor availability and interaction networks as strategies for therapeutically modulating RNA editing.

abstract: The investigators propose a pilot randomized trial to gather preliminary data to test the hypothesis that Fisetin will reduce abundance of senescent cells in blood, skeletal muscle, and both subcutaneous and inter muscular adipose tissue and improve 6-minute walk distance in 34 people with peripheral artery disease (PAD). the investigators will determine whether greater declines in abundance of cells with senescent markers are associated with greater improvement in 6-minute walk distance in people with peripheral artery disease. In exploratory analyses, the investigators will assess whether Fisetin reduces interleukin-6 (IL-6) and novel senescent markers in adipose tissue, muscle, and/or blood.
description:
Fisetin is a flavanol, present in strawberries, apples, and persimmons, that destroys senescent cells (i.e. a senolytic therapy). Of three senolytic therapies being tested in clinical trials, Fisetin has the best safety profile. Hence, the investigators propose a pilot randomized trial to gather preliminary data to test the hypothesis that Fisetin will reduce abundance of senescent cells in blood, skeletal muscle, and both subcutaneous and inter muscular adipose tissue and improve 6-minute walk distance in 34 people with PAD. The investigators will determine whether greater declines in abundance of cells with senescent markers are associated with greater improvement in 6-minute walk distance in people with PAD. In exploratory analyses, the investigators will assess whether Fisetin reduces IL-6 and novel senescent markers in adipose tissue, muscle, and/or blood.

To achieve the trial's specific aims, investigators will randomize 34 participants age 50 and older with PAD to one of two groups: Fisetin vs placebo. Participants will be followed for four months.

abstract: The primary objective will be to demonstrate the manufacturing feasibility and safety, and to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of RNA-LP vaccines in pediatric patients with recurrent/progressive Medulloblastoma (MB)

institutions.label: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium

description:
This is a first in human Phase I study of RNA-LP vaccines for pediatric patients with recurrent/progressive Medulloblastoma (MB). The phase I portion of the study will involve a dose-escalation study to identify the maximally tolerated dose (MTD).

This clinical trial will consist of three parts: Surgery, Salvage Therapy (Radiation and/or chemotherapy), and Immunotherapy. Potentially eligible participants will be enrolled on a screening consent for the sterile collection of tumor material in a manner suitable for RNA extraction, amplification, and loading of lipid particles (LPs). Pediatric participants will have tumor material sent to the University of Florida (UF) from qualified PNOC sites. Following surgical resection with confirmatory pathologic diagnosis, patients will be enrolled in the trial after informed consent has been obtained.

The RNA-LP vaccination will begin within 4 weeks following salvage therapy and after review of post-radiation MRI (for baseline). After radiation patients will receive three RNA-LP vaccines every 2 weeks before beginning 12 cycles of adjuvant monthly RNA- LP vaccines for a total of 15 vaccines.

Participants may receive RNA-LP vaccines for up to 14 months.

Participants will be followed until death due to any cause. MRI and clinical evaluation for assessment of disease progression will be conducted every 3 months for the first-year post-immunotherapy.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) have revolutionized nucleic acid therapeutics, yet their clinical success relies heavily on precise manufacturing processes. This review comprehensively explores the critical intersection between microfluidic channel design, lipid self-assembly biophysics, and the subsequent biological performance of mRNA-LNPs. First, we analyze the fundamental fluid mechanics driving representative microfluidic mixers, elucidating how different channel architectures dictate solvent exchange rates and nanoparticle assembly kinetics. We then systematically examine how these specific mixing regimes modulate essential physicochemical characteristics, including lipid distribution, internal nanostructure, particle morphology, size distribution, and overall colloidal stability. Crucially, we bridge the gap between manufacturing and pharmacology by evaluating how mixing-induced physicochemical differences directly translate into distinct biological outcomes, such as cellular uptake mechanisms, endosomal escape efficiency, and systemic pharmacokinetics. By integrating microfluidic engineering principles with biological evaluation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how continuous-flow assembly processes program the functional behavior of mRNA-LNP systems. Ultimately, we highlight emerging design principles essential for developing the next generation of robust, highly efficient nucleic acid delivery platforms.

abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100-1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.
