abstract: The aged tumor microenvironment can impair antitumor T-cell function, but the molecular regulators that become limiting in this setting remain poorly defined. In a recent issue of Cell, Chen and colleagues harness in vivo CRISPR screening to compare the effects of genetic perturbations in tumor-reactive CD8+ T cells across young and aged hosts. The screen reveals that increased T-cell persistence or an effector-like transcriptional state does not necessarily translate into improved tumor control and identifies Dusp5 and Zfp219 as distinct functional regulators. DUSP5 broadly restrains ERK-dependent proliferation, and its loss improves tumor control in both young and aged mice. ZFP219, by contrast, preferentially limits cytotoxicity in aged hosts; its deletion increases granzyme expression and improves tumor control specifically in the aged setting. Human tumor datasets show that ZNF219 expression in intratumoral CD8+ T cells increases with age and is associated with poorer clinical outcomes. Moreover, Zfp219 loss enhances the response to PD-1 blockade in aged mice, producing complete tumor clearance in a subset of animals and durable protection after rechallenge. Together, these findings show that host age can reshape the functional consequences of T-cell perturbations and reveal age-dependent genetic vulnerabilities with potential therapeutic relevance.

title: Aging Rewires Genetic Dependencies in Antitumor T Cells.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8+ T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity.
RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

abstract: The goal of this randomized clinical trial is to be adequately powered to evaluate the effect of ketogenic metabolic therapy on the quality of life in serious mental illness, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder.
description:
The ketogenic diet is a low carbohydrate, moderate protein, higher fat diet to help individuals improve energy and mood and to obtain nutrients from fats and protein. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder, collectively affect about 344 million individuals worldwide, (24 million with schizophrenia, 40 million people with BD, and 280 million with depression World Health Organization). These illnesses are debilitating psychiatric conditions characterized by a chronic pattern of emotional, behavioral, and cognitive disturbances. Shared psychopathology includes the pre-eminence of altered affective states, disorders of thoughts, and behavioral control. Additionally, those conditions share epidemiological traits, including significant cardiovascular, metabolic, infectious, and respiratory comorbidities, resulting in reduced life expectancy of up to 25 years (Xie et al., 2023). Reductions in cerebral glucose uptake are seen in both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. While glucose is the brain's default fuel, ketone bodies are 27% more efficient, improve brain metabolism, and promote neural stability, as seen in childhood epilepsy (Sethi \& Ford, 2022). The ketogenic diet (KD, also known as metabolic therapy) has been successful in the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and epilepsy (Sethi et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2018, Martin-McGill et al., 2020). Nutritional ketosis has been successfully used to treat a range of neurological disorders. Metabolic disorders, which include conditions such as obesity and metabolic syndrome, more commonly occur in individuals with severe mental illness (between 40-60%). The investigators aim to study the effect of ketogenic metabolic therapy on various markers including:

* Metabolic health measurements and cardiovascular risk factors including: insulin resistance, advanced lipid analysis, weight, glucose regulation, dyslipidemia, absolute body fat chang, inflammation, waist circumference, blood pressure, skeletal muscle mass, and omega index
* Psychiatric symptom measures include: mood, psychosis, cognition, and quality of life
* Deep omic profiling including metabolic and proteomic data. Through identifying patterns, changes, and pathways of molecular, psychiatric, physiologic, and metabolic markers, the investigators aim to assess how this intervention may impact individuals with serious mental illnesses and symptoms/conditions related to serious mental illnesses.

abstract: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are pivotal for antigen recognition within germinal centers (GCs), which are essential for B-cell maturation and high-affinity antibody production. Although the role played by T follicular helper (Tfh) cells in supporting B cells is established, the mechanisms driving the expansion and maintenance of distinct T-cell clonotypes in the GC perifollicular region remain poorly understood. This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on the differentiation, migration, and clonal expansion of T cells within GCs, with emphasis on Tfh-B-cell interactions. Findings from immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiphoton microscopy, and CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches indicate that clonal expansion of T cells carrying defined TCR clonotypes is a regulated process driven by cognate Tfh-B-cell interactions. These interactions promote both B-cell affinity maturation and the concomitant selection and clonal expansion of T cells. The reviewed studies reveal that the TCR repertoire within the GC perifollicular region is refined over time, contributing to the development of long-lived memory and effector cells. The collective results underscore a dynamic reciprocity where T cells shape the antibody response while themselves undergoing antigen-driven selection. Key challenges include clarifying TCR signaling networks, improving in vivo analysis of cellular interactions, and identifying strategies to therapeutically modulate these processes without disrupting immune homeostasis. Overcoming these hurdles will require interdisciplinary approaches and the application of emerging technologies. Future research focused on these areas will be critical for advancing fundamental immunology and developing novel therapeutic strategies for vaccines, autoimmune diseases, and cancer.

title: T-cell clonality and TCR repertoire dynamics during germinal center responses: A comprehensive review of regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.

abstract: PARP1 is a crucial enzyme involved in DNA-damage repair and other biological processes through poly(ADP-ribose) modification (PARylation), but persistent activation can trigger parthanatos. Despite extensive research, the precise mechanisms governing PARP1 activity remain elusive. Here, through multiple CRISPR-Cas9 screens, we identified NAXE, an NADH hydrate (NADHX) epimerase, as a key regulator of PARP1 activity homeostasis. We show that NADHX inhibits PARP1-DNA binding, while NAXE lowers NADHX levels to promote PARP1 recruitment and DNA repair. PARP1 activation, in turn, induces PARylation that binds and inhibits NAXE, forming a negative feedback loop that restrains PARP1 aberrant activation. Notably, knockout of NAXE in mice and C. elegans disrupts PARylation homeostasis, leading to sustained DNA damage and PARP1 activation, ultimately resulting in parthanatos-driven catastrophic neural injury. These findings uncover a metabolite-mediated feedback mechanism that preserves PARylation homeostasis and highlight NAXE as a potential therapeutic target in PARP1-related neurological disorders.

abstract: Within the tumor microenvironment (TME), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play an important role in liver cancer progression through intercellular communication, including the release of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs). This study investigated the potential mechanisms underlying the effects of CAF-associated miR-483-5p on liver cancer progression. sEV-enriched preparations were isolated from CAFs transfected with a miR-483-5p mimic or an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and subsequently used to treat HepG2 cells. These preparations were designated as CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-mimic and CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-ASO, respectively. To evaluate cell proliferation and stemness, colony formation and spheroid formation assays were applied. Additionally, a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was established to assess the in vivo effects of these CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations. MiR-483-5p enhanced HepG2 cell proliferation, stemness, and migration, and higher miR-483-5p expression was associated with poorer patient prognosis. CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations was associated with increased miR-483-5p levels in HepG2 cells, suggesting that these preparations may contribute to the regulation of miR-483-5p levels in recipient cells. The CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p mimic preparation promoted HepG2 cell proliferation and stemness while suppressing apoptosis. Luciferase reporter and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) assays supported the direct interaction between miR-483-5p and the Modulator of apoptosis 1 (MOAP1) 3' untranslated region (3'-UTR) and showed that miR-483-5p negatively regulates MOAP1 expression. MOAP1 downregulation was associated with increased proliferation and stemness in HepG2 cells. Importantly, MOAP1 overexpression attenuated miR-483-5p-induced increases in proliferation, migration, and stemness in HepG2 cells, as well as the upregulation of Wnt1, β-catenin, Nanog, Sox2, and Oct4. Furthermore, miR-483-5p ASO reversed the effects of CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations on miR-483-5p levels, MOAP1 expression, and HepG2 cell viability. In vivo, the CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-mimic preparation promoted xenograft tumor growth in nude mice. Collectively, CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations may contribute to increased miR-483-5p levels and promote the growth and stemness of liver cancer cells, potentially through miR-483-5p-mediated downregulation of MOAP1. These findings suggest that the miR-483-5p/MOAP1 regulatory axis may serve as a potential therapeutic target for liver cancer.

abstract: The emergence of mRNA vaccines and therapeutics demands robust analytical methods not only for biophysical characterization of their complex structures but also for assessing biological activity to reflect therapeutic function. This article describes the development of two complementary cell-based potency assays to analyze both protein expression and enzymatic activity of an mRNA-LNP (lipid nanoparticle) drug candidate for treating glycogen storage disease type III (GSDIII). An In-Cell Western (ICW) assay and a glycogen debranching enzyme (GDE) enzymatic activity assay were developed and optimized using HepG2 AGL KO cells, with human serum pre-treatment to enhance cellular uptake. Both methods demonstrated excellent assay performance, with accuracy between 80% and 120% and precision below 15% across their respective linear ranges. Additionally, the two assays also yielded comparable results when testing drug product (DP) samples with varying potency levels. Finally, potency assays detected decline in GDE protein expression and enzymatic activity in thermally stressed samples. These results correlate to mRNA degradation measured via capillary electrophoresis (CE), whereas the mRNA-LNP particle size and encapsulation efficiency remain unchanged. These findings demonstrate that cell-based potency assays are not only stability-indicating methods but also essential tools for analyzing the functional aspects of mRNA therapeutics, with broader applicability beyond this GSDIII case study.

abstract: Rapid advances in disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) for epilepsy, including gene-based therapies, antisense oligonucleotides, and stem cell-derived approaches, are reshaping the treatment landscape. As these therapies move through clinical trials and toward regulatory review, they introduce complex clinical, operational, ethical, and equity considerations that extend well beyond traditional antiseizure medication management. Successful integration will require careful attention to patient selection, genetic and biomarker testing, multidisciplinary care models, infrastructure readiness, referral pathways, long-term safety monitoring, informed consent for novel and potentially irreversible interventions, access to clinical trials, and cost and reimbursement challenges. Significant investments in personnel, systems, and facilities may be necessary, raising important questions about implementation across diverse practice settings and the risk of widening disparities in care. Here, we review the evolving therapeutic pipeline and outline key considerations for safe, ethical, and equitable implementation.

title: Beyond Seizure Control: Building the Infrastructure for Disease-Modifying Therapies in Epilepsy.

abstract: Protein biologics are constrained in critical-size bone defects not by insufficient potency, but by rapid clearance and the inability to sustain therapeutic signaling at the repair site. Dose escalation does not overcome this pharmacokinetic limitation and instead increases the risk of ectopic bone formation, osteolysis, and soft tissue toxicity. Sustained, localized delivery, not higher dosing, is the unmet requirement. Gene-activated matrices (GAM) address this problem by integrating nucleic acid cargo and delivery vectors within an implantable scaffold, converting infiltrating host cells into local sources of regenerative signals. This review examines GAMs as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration, tracing their development from scaffold bioactivity and the limitation of protein biologics to nucleic acid-based delivery. We compare viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric polyplexes, calcium phosphate nanoparticles, and scaffold-integrated systems across transduction efficiency, expression kinetics, immunogenicity, and bone-site retention. We then examine how scaffold composition, architecture, and fabrication govern vector retention, release, and substrate-mediated transfection. This review then evaluates nucleic acid cargo selection and coordinated osteogenic and angiogenic gene delivery, including pDNA, mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, and explores emerging multi-factor, stimuli-responsive, and CRISPR-based GAMs alongside their translational constraints. A distinct feature of this review is its claim-level patent analysis, which identifies substantial intellectual-property white space in GAM development. Despite strong preclinical evidence, no GAM platform has simultaneously achieved scalable manufacturing, regulatory readiness as a combination product, and validation in a human-scale bone defect model. Clinical translation will require coordinated optimization of vector-scaffold interactions, manufacturing scalability, safety, and clinically relevant validation.

title: Gene-activated matrices as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration: Delivery, translation and patent landscape.

abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) serve as pivotal mediators bridging innate immunity and neuroinflammation, orchestrating pathological cascades that drive neurological disorders. Beyond their sentinel role in pathogen recognition, aberrant TLR activation triggers intricate and destructive signaling networks, including activation of NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, alongside IRFs and type I interferon responses that converge on chronic neuroinflammation and subsequent neuronal damage. This review dissects TLRs' multilayered contribution to neuropathology, emphasizing their regulation of secondary inflammatory mechanisms, including NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation, mTOR-driven metabolic dysregulation, SOCS-mediated feedback inhibition, inflammasome activation, and pyroptotic cell death. Critically, these signaling pathways create a pathological intersection with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, amplifying a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury that underlies conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Stroke, Multiple sclerosis (MS), Epilepsy and Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Against this neuropathological landscape, this review systematically evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TLR-mediated neuroinflammation, encompassing small molecule TLR antagonists, intracellular adaptor protein inhibitors targeting myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) and TIR-domain-containing adapter-inducing interferon-β (TRIF), biologic therapies including monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins, natural phytochemicals and nutraceuticals, Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genomic interventions, and cell-based immunomodulatory therapies, collectively representing a mechanistically diverse arsenal aimed at recalibrating the dysregulated innate immune response to achieve durable neuroprotection across the full spectrum of TLR-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Toll-Like Receptor-Driven Neuroinflammation in Neurological Disorders: Signaling Crosstalk and Therapeutic Opportunities.

abstract: RNA-based therapies are providing new ways to treat infections, cancer, and inherited diseases. These therapies fall into two broad categories: non-replicating RNAs, like messenger RNA, small interfering RNA (siRNA), and antisense oligonucleotides; and replicating RNAs, such as self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) and defective interfering (DI) RNAs. Non-replicating RNAs act in a single round and depend on precise chemical design and effective delivery. Replicating RNAs make more copies of themselves inside cells directly or conditionally, which can improve their strength, duration, and ability to trigger immune responses. In this review, we compare how these two groups of RNA therapies work, how they are designed and delivered, and where they are best suited. We discuss differences in immune effects, dosing, and manufacturing, and include long-studied DI RNAs, now being developed as a new type of antiviral therapy with broad activity and a favorable emerging preclinical safety profile. We also explore delivery methods such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and polymer-based systems. By comparing replicating and non-replicating strategies, we aim to clarify their roles in RNA medicine and highlight how they might be combined in future treatments.

title: Replicating vs. non-replicating RNA therapeutics: Mechanisms, trade-offs, and future directions.

abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vectors have moved central nervous system (CNS) gene therapy from experimental proof of concept to clinically validated treatment, yet therapeutic design remains highly dependent on disease mechanism, cellular distribution, and treatment timing. This narrative review examines recent progress in rAAV-based interventions for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) and neurodegenerative disorders. For monogenic NDDs, gene replacement is most applicable to loss-of-function conditions with compatible payload size and tolerable expression, whereas dominant-negative, gain-of-function, and dosage-sensitive disorders may require allele-selective silencing or precise DNA or RNA editing. Rett syndrome illustrates both the reversibility of postnatal dysfunction and the need for tightly regulated transgene expression. Spinal muscular atrophy provides the leading translational paradigm: rAAV9-mediated SMN1 replacement demonstrates the value of early diagnosis, adequate tissue exposure, and treatment before irreversible neuronal loss. For complex neurodegenerative diseases, emerging strategies extend beyond simple gene addition. APOE-directed editing and protective-variant replacement may enable genotype-informed intervention in Alzheimer's disease, whereas Parkinson's disease programs combine restoration of dopamine synthesis, neuroprotection, and genetically encoded circuit modulation. Across these indications, major barriers include incomplete and nonselective CNS delivery, immune and dose-related toxicity, limited redosing, durable control of transgene or editor activity, off-target effects, and uncertain translation from animal models to humans. Progress over the next decade will depend on human-compatible vectors, cell-selective and regulatable expression, rigorous long-term safety assessment, biomarker-guided trials, and rational combinations that connect molecular target engagement to meaningful neurological benefit.

title: Recombinant AAV-Based Gene Therapy for Central Nervous System Disorders: From Gene Replacement to Precision Editing and Circuit Modulation.

abstract: State-of-the-art techniques using synthetic antisense oligonucleotides and other nucleotide-based therapeutics have transformed treatment for a wide range of diseases, including neurological, metabolic, cardiovascular, and muscular disorders, many of which were previously incurable. As the biopharmaceutical industry expands into this new therapeutic field, there is increasing demand for robust purification and analytical techniques. Therapeutic oligonucleotides are most often purified by ion pair-reversed phase (IP-RP) and anion-exchange (AEX) chromatography techniques. Here, we present a single-step chromatography approach utilizing hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) for a 5'-dimethoxytrityl (5'-DMT)-protected 20-mer single-stranded DNA oligonucleotide. The HIC process incorporates an optimized on-column detritylation step at pH 4.0, enabling removal of the 5'-DMT protective cap from the purified oligonucleotide. This method also effectively eliminated the majority of < 20-mer oligonucleotide impurities, which were present as deprotected oligonucleotides in the crude starting material. Analytical RP and AEX chromatography methods confirmed nearly complete (99.6%) 5'-DMT removal and an oligonucleotide recovery rate of 96.9% for the final product. Moreover, an RP chromatographic depurination assay demonstrated that the acidic detritylation procedure did not result in detrimental adenine or guanine purine base loss. The all-aqueous HIC process is environmentally friendly and avoids the flammability risks associated with RP technique.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 has transformed agricultural biotechnology, microbial engineering, and human therapeutics within a decade, yet biosafety assessment remains focused on editing accuracy and off-target cleavage. A second, neglected question is what the high-molecular-weight Cas9 effector protein does to expressing systems. This review integrates evidence from eukaryotic cell lines, microbial hosts, transgenic mammals, and dietary exposure models. In isolated cells Cas9 injures the host by three routes, only one requiring DNA cleavage: TP53-dependent genotoxic stress at susceptible loci, modified by cell sex and p53 status; guide-independent binding to ribosomal proteins that activates the PI3K-mTORC2 axis; and promiscuous association with host transcripts inducing a p53-linked stress programme. In GC-rich bacteria, PAM density and limited double-strand break repair make basal expression lethal. Intact mammals tolerate tissue-restricted Cas9 expression, although nervous system and germline compartments are exceptions, and dietary exposure carries no measurable toxicological or allergenic risk. Pre-existing anti-Cas9 immunity is the dominant translational barrier. Proteasomal, SUMO-regulated and autophagic pathways together set Cas9 half-life. Transient ribonucleoprotein delivery, anti-CRISPR, degron-based control, and lower-toxicity orthogonal nucleases each narrow this exposure window. We conclude that Cas9 toxicity is not intrinsic but contingent on expression kinetics, delivery format, host repair, proteostatic capacity, and immunological history. Biosafety is therefore a tunable design parameter, and this review provides a mechanism-based framework for matching nuclease, delivery route and temporal control to the intended application.

abstract: The Hippo-YAP/TEAD signaling axis regulates tissue growth, cellular identity, and organ homeostasis. Dysregulation of this pathway, through NF2 loss, LATS1 or LATS2 inactivation, or YAP1- or WWTR1-derived gene fusions, results in persistent nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ, driving TEAD-dependent transcriptional programs. NF2-deficient and YAP1/TAZ-driven tumors, such as mesothelioma, schwannoma, meningioma, and epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, exemplify Hippo-pathway dependency and are potential therapeutic targets. Targeting TEAD disrupts transcriptional circuits sustaining tumor growth, plasticity, and immune suppression while modulating metabolic and stromal dependencies. Pharmacologic interventions targeting YAP/TEAD include TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors, direct YAP/TEAD protein-protein interaction disruptors, PROTAC-mediated TEAD degraders, and YAP-directed antisense oligonucleotide strategies. Early-phase trials have demonstrated preliminary clinical activity, particularly with TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors in mesothelioma and have been associated with mild drug-related toxicities, such as proteinuria. YAP/TEAD inhibition may also be a rational combinatorial approach given the emergence of adaptive resistance mechanisms to EGFR/KRAS inhibitors and immunotherapies. Collectively, these findings provide rationale and early proof-of-concept for the pharmacologic targeting of the YAP/TEAD pathway. In this review, we describe the biological underpinnings of the YAP/TEAD pathway in cancer medicine, the anti-cancer strategies targeting this pathway, and discuss future directions in the field.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mucin-type O-GalNAc glycosylation mediated by N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase (GALNT) family enzymes contributes to tumor progression, while GALNT14's functional substrates and mechanisms in TNBC remain largely unknown.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Expression profiling was performed using clinical tissue microarray and TCGA dataset. Cellular loss-of-function, gain-of-function and rescue experiments were conducted in TNBC cell lines. In vivo tumor growth and lung metastasis were evaluated in nude mice. Co-IP-LC-MS/MS, VVA-lectin pulldown and cycloheximide-chase assays were applied to identify interacting partners, characterize O-GalNAc glycosylation and assess protein stability.
RESULTS: GALNT14 was markedly upregulated in TNBC tissues (P < 0.05). GALNT14 knockdown inhibited TNBC cell proliferation, migration and invasion in vitro (P < 0.001), and suppressed xenograft growth and lung metastasis in vivo (tumor weight: P < 0.001; metastatic nodules: P < 0.01). α-Enolase 1 (ENO1) was identified as a novel substrate of GALNT14. GALNT14 catalyzed O-GalNAc glycosylation of ENO1 at Ser63. This modification did not change ENO1 mRNA level, yet enhanced ENO1 protein stability (P < 0.001). Under GALNT14-proficient background, glycosylation-deficient ENO1-S63A displayed attenuated oncogenic capacity compared with ENO1-WT (P < 0.05). Both ENO1-WT and ENO1-S63A rescued malignant phenotypes upon GALNT14 silencing (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: A GALNT14-ENO1 Ser63 O-GalNAc glycosylation axis drives TNBC progression, providing new mechanistic insight and candidate therapeutic targets for TNBC.

abstract: In recent years, the increase in poor lifestyle and dietary habits (such as smoking, unhealthy eating) coupled with the high prevalence of chronic comorbidities including diabetes and hypertension has led to a rising number of patients with kidney disease. Kidney transplantation (KT), as an important means to improve the quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), has been widely applied in clinical treatment. However, post-kidney transplantation urinary tract infections (Post-KT UTIs), as a serious postoperative complication, severely threatens the safety of transplant recipients and the long-term function of grafts. Post-KT UTIs refer to an inflammatory reaction resulting from pathogen proliferation in the urinary system after transplantation, which may include cystitis, pyelonephritis, and in severe instances, can advance to bacteremia or sepsis, endangering both patient and graft survival. Post-KT UTIs are commonly caused by Gram-negative bacterial infections, notably by species such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Currently, the clinical detection and treatment of Post-KT UTIs remain based primarily on traditional urine culture and empirical antimicrobial therapy. This review introduces advanced detection methods such as next-generation sequencing and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), aiming to offer new strategies for diagnosing Post-KT UTIs. Moreover, it reviews recent advancements in the epidemiology, treatment methods, and preventive strategies of Post-KT UTIs, and the role of gut and urinary microbiota in infection development, aiming to facilitate the development of novel therapeutic agents, vaccine formulations, and refined treatment strategies for precise management of Post-KT UTIs.

abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

abstract: Sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous RNA in living cells remains challenging because of insufficient signal amplification, background activation, and interference between parallel readout pathways, particularly for low-abundance regulatory RNAs. Many current CRISPR-based RNA imaging strategies rely on stoichiometric RNA binding, limiting sensitivity and often yielding a poor signal-to-background ratio for low-abundance endogenous microRNAs (miRNAs). Moreover, limited orthogonality between sensing modules and readouts complicates interference-free multiplexing. Inefficient intracellular delivery further limits their applicability in complex biological environments. Here, we introduce an allosteric CRISPR probe for orthogonal and amplified miRNA imaging in living cells, which is built on an allosterically gated crRNA that integrates a CRISPR-Cas12a system with a Zn2+-dependent DNAzyme module. Mechanistically, miR-210 selectively unlocks the caged crRNA to activate Cas12a trans-cleavage, providing amplified red (Cy5) fluorescence, while miR-21 independently activates DNAzyme cleavage to generate green (FAM) fluorescence with minimal cross-talk. Black phosphorus nanosheets serve as a biocompatible nanocarrier for efficient intracellular probe delivery. This orthogonal architecture enables precise discrimination of breast cancer subtypes in living cells and clinical tissue sections. Together, this work overcomes a central limitation of live-cell miRNA imaging by enabling sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous miRNAs, opening new possibilities for dissecting RNA-mediated regulation in complex cellular systems.

abstract: Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is a next-generation nucleic acid vaccine platform that enhances antigen expression through intracellular amplification of replicon RNA without producing infectious virions. saRNA constructs encode an alphavirus-derived replicase comprising nonstructural proteins nsP1-nsP4 and can elicit robust immune responses at low RNA doses. Replication intermediates may activate RIG-I, MDA5, and endosomal TLR3/7/8, contributing adjuvant-like activity. Kostaive (ARCT-154; zapomeran) became the first saRNA vaccine to receive full marketing approval in Japan in 2023, followed by authorization in the European Union in 2025 and the United Kingdom in 2026, demonstrating the platform's clinical and regulatory feasibility. Development now extends beyond COVID-19 to seasonal and pandemic influenza, rabies, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Nipah virus disease, and individualized cancer vaccines. However, the longer transcripts and additional replicase and subgenomic-promoter elements make in vitro transcription efficiency, full-length RNA content, double-stranded and truncated RNA impurities, lipid nanoparticle encapsulation, and potency testing particularly important. Regulatory assessment increasingly focuses on correct replicase and antigen expression, the magnitude and duration of self-amplification, biodistribution and persistence, and comparability. This review synthesizes the scientific basis, development landscape, manufacturing challenges, and regulatory science considerations of saRNA vaccines.

title: Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccines After the First Approvals: Technology, Development Landscape, and Regulatory Science Considerations.

abstract: Atherosclerosis remains the principal pathological substrate of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke and peripheral artery disease, and its progression is driven by an interlocking set of processes, including hepatic and vascular lipid metabolism, chronic vascular inflammation, macrophage foam cell formation and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation, none of which is fully controlled by currently approved pharmacotherapy. Short hairpin RNA (shRNA) technology, in which a DNA template encoding a stem-loop transcript is delivered to a cell and processed intracellularly into small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that trigger sequence-specific mRNA degradation, offers a route to durable, vector-encoded gene silencing that is mechanistically distinct from transiently acting synthetic siRNA or antisense oligonucleotides and that, although non-permanent at the level of the target gene, is not readily reversible at the level of the vector, which cannot easily be withdrawn once administered. This review analyzes the current status of shRNA-based strategies for atherosclerosis therapy. We summarize the molecular mechanism and vector design principles of shRNA-mediated RNA interference (RNAi); critically examine preclinical studies in which shRNA delivered by lentiviral or adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors has been used to silence hepatic lipid-metabolism genes (PCSK9, ApoB,), the endothelial gene ANGPTL2, inflammasome and inflammatory mediators (NLRP3, TACE/ADAM17), and genes driving VSMC proliferation in restenosis models (connexin 43); we explicitly distinguish this direct shRNA evidence from complementary target-validation studies that use antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., ANGPTL4), synthetic siRNA, genetic knockout, or antimiR approaches (e.g., lncRNA AK136714, CD36, miR-33, P2X7R); and discuss the principal delivery vectors, their tissue tropism, and the toxicity arising from saturation of the endogenous microRNA-processing machinery. We further place shRNA in the context of competing and complementary RNA-based and gene-editing modalities, including clinically approved synthetic siRNA drugs (inclisiran, patisiran) and CRISPR-based gene editing of PCSK9 and ANGPTL3, both of which have now yielded human phase 1 data, to clarify why, despite two decades of robust preclinical proof-of-concept, no shRNA construct has yet reached clinical use in atherosclerosis; we further compare this with the clinical trajectory of vector-encoded shRNA in other indications, in which anti-CCR5 and anti-HCV constructs have already been administered to patients in phase 1/2 trials, in order to establish that the limiting factor is not the hairpin itself but the risk-benefit case obtainable in a chronic, largely asymptomatic disease for which withdrawable and outcome-validated therapies already exist. We conclude that shRNA remains a mechanistically attractive but clinically immature modality whose translation will depend on vector engineering that limits off-target saturation of the RNAi pathway and achieves durable, cell type-restricted expression in the liver, endothelium, macrophages or vascular wall, and, equally, on the identification of an atherosclerosis indication-most plausibly a small, high-residual-risk or locally treatable population-in which durability outweighs the vector-level irreversibility, immunogenicity and manufacturing burden of a viral vector.

title: Analysis of the Use of shRNA in Atherosclerosis Therapy: Current Status.

abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have evolved into a significant delivery technology for nucleic acid therapies, including messenger RNA (mRNA), small interfering RNA (siRNA), and genome editing tools. Although LNPs have demonstrated therapeutic success, they display strong tropism to the liver when systemically delivered, thus restricting their use for targeted delivery to extrahepatic organs. The major factor responsible for the liver targeting of LNPs is the binding of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to the nanoparticle surface, which enables their recognition by lipoprotein receptors and uptake by liver cells. However, increasing evidence suggests that the tropism of LNPs can be altered by controlling lipid composition, physical and chemical properties, and acquired biological properties. This review discusses the mechanisms responsible for the liver tropism of LNPs as well as recent trends in modulating LNP tropism to extrahepatic organs. How ionizable lipids, helper lipids and sterols, PEG-lipids, LNP properties, and interaction with the protein corona can impact the organ tropism of LNPs as well as approaches for active and endogenous targeting of LNPs for organ- and cell-specific delivery are discussed. The challenges associated with organ- and cell-selective delivery of nucleic acids, such as delivery to functionally specific cell populations, endosomal release, species-specific translation, safety, repeated dosing, and clinical translation, are also described.

title: Engineering Lipid Nanoparticles Beyond ApoE-Mediated Liver Tropism: Design Strategies for Extrahepatic and Organ-Selective Delivery.

abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are promising platforms for regenerative and immunomodulatory therapies, but their clinical performance is limited by donor heterogeneity, variable potency, and limited persistence. CRISPR-based engineering provides programmable approaches to modify MSC function through genome editing and transcriptional regulation. This review examines CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout and knock-in, dCas9-based transcriptional regulation, and emerging base-, prime-, and epigenome-editing technologies for MSC engineering. These approaches can enhance survival and stress resistance, homing and tissue retention, paracrine and extracellular vesicle activity, immunomodulation, immune compatibility, and lineage-associated functions. Key translational challenges include efficient delivery, engineered-population heterogeneity, genomic safety, immunogenicity, phenotypic stability, scalable manufacturing, and mechanism-linked potency assessment. The appropriate engineering strategy should therefore be selected according to the intended therapeutic mechanism and product development requirements. Clinical translation will ultimately depend on demonstrating reproducible functional enhancement, manufacturing consistency, genomic and phenotypic stability, and validated therapeutic potency.

title: CRISPR-Based Engineering of Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Functional Enhancement, Translational Challenges, and Clinical Perspectives.

abstract: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.

abstract: Tumor cells possess nucleic-acid sensing systems that detect aberrant DNA and RNA arising from genomic and transcriptomic dysregulation. Cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors, together with endosomal nucleic acid sensors, can induce type I interferons, inflammatory chemokines, antigen presentation programs, and immune cell recruitment. Yet many tumors remain immunologically silent despite harboring potentially immunostimulatory nucleic acids, indicating that malignant cells can restrain these pathways at multiple levels. Nucleic acid clearance, selective RNA editing and remodeling, extracellular second messenger degradation, and epigenetic silencing can suppress these responses. These regulatory layers may favor immune-poor tumor states and limit responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Therapeutic reactivation must be spatially and temporally controlled, because persistent signaling can undergo maladaptive rewiring. We review these molecular brakes, therapeutic strategies to restore innate sensing, and a proposed biomarker framework integrating sensor competence, suppressor activity, and functional immune output. We distinguish the effects arising within tumor cells from those mediated by sensing mechanisms in neighboring host cells and discuss cellular and spatial context, signaling dynamics, and safety. The proposed framework for matching treatments to patients remains investigational and requires prospective clinical validation.

abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1-targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics have transformed cancer treatment strategies, especially after the success of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled mRNA vaccines. LNPs are effective non-viral delivery vehicles that protect mRNA, enhance intracellular delivery, and improve therapeutic safety. This review discusses recent advancements in LNP-mediated mRNA therapies, including mRNA vaccines, cytokine delivery, immune modulation, and CAR-based strategies. Innovations in lipid formulations and high-throughput technologies have enhanced delivery efficiency. We also discussed how LNP-mRNA formulations elicit immune responses and improve tumor microenvironments. We highlight promising personalized mRNA vaccines and therapies. However, challenges such as tissue specificity, immunogenicity, and manufacturing remain. Emerging strategies in lipid engineering and personalized medicine aim to address these issues, making LNP-mediated mRNA therapeutics a pivotal approach in precision oncology. This report provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in LNP-mRNA therapeutics for cancer treatment. This report also highlights recent innovations and clinical trials. We further highlight the limitations and challenges associated with LNP-mRNA therapeutics in clinical translation. Finally, we outlined the prospects of LNP-based mRNA therapeutics for personalized cancer treatment.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA delivery system for cancer management.

abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.

abstract: The CRISPR-Cas12a system has revolutionized molecular diagnostics; however, the strict requirement of crRNAs and target DNA for collateral cleavage activation restricts its flexibility in non-nucleic acid diagnostics. Herein, we demonstrate that AsCas12a exhibits an RNA-free collateral cleavage activity with the presence of manganese ions (Mn2+), which preferentially cleaves single-stranded DNA efficiently. Mechanistically, kinetic analyses reveal that AsCas12a exhibits a significantly higher binding affinity for Mn2+ than for magnesium ion (Mg2+), while molecular dynamics simulations suggest that Mn2+ coordination induces conformational changes to expose the RuvC endonuclease domain. Harnessing this unique property, an enzymatic cascade-amplified electrochemical biosensor integrating manganese nanoflowers is reported for the diagnosis of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast cancer. By equipping screen-printed gold electrodes with DNA reporters, this diagnostic tool enables high-precision HER2 quantification and successfully distinguishes various HER2-related cell lines. Furthermore, the biosensor has been extended to analyze HER2-positive exosomes, facilitating the dynamic tracking of serum exosome levels in tumor-bearing nude mice to evaluate therapeutic efficacy and accurately distinguish HER2-positive breast cancer patients in clinical samples. This RNA-free Cas12a system may provide new insights into CRISPR-based non-nucleic acid detection, emerging as a powerful tool for dynamic tumor monitoring and precision oncology.

title: CRISPR-AsCas12a with crRNA-Free Collateral Cleavage Activity for Electrochemical Diagnosis of HER2-Positive Breast Cancer.

abstract: RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

title: SecAntiGami: A Secondary-Antibody-Inspired RNA Origami for Qualitative Aptamer Validation.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance.
RESULTS: In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening.
AVAILABILITY: The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: PRIDA: Cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning.

abstract: Earliness and plant architecture are major breeding targets in cucurbit crops because they influence crop duration, early yield, planting density, canopy management, and production efficiency. This review summarizes genetic, molecular, and genome-editing advances related to flowering, sex expression, fruit development, stem elongation, branching, and canopy architecture in cucumber, melon, watermelon, Cucurbita species, and other cucurbits. Current evidence shows that earlier flowering or increased femaleness does not necessarily lead to earlier commercial maturity, while compact growth must be evaluated together with yield, fruit quality, and environmental adaptation. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout remains the most established editing approach, whereas base editing, cis-regulatory editing, multiplex editing, developmental-regulator-assisted regeneration, and DNA-free RNP delivery offer promising routes toward more precise trait optimization. Major constraints include genotype-dependent transformation, pleiotropic effects, limited validation in elite germplasm, and scarce direct evidence for shortening fruit-development duration. An evidence-guided framework is proposed that links trait definition, functional genomics, target prioritization, tailored genome editing, whole-plant evaluation, and breeding deployment. Future progress will depend on quantitatively tuned alleles and coordinated optimization of reproductive timing, canopy architecture, productivity, fruit quality, and environmental stability.

abstract: As the primary cash crop for natural fiber, cotton develops under sophisticated endogenous genetic programs, with biotic and abiotic stresses continuously driving its adaptive evolution. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional regulators that modulate gene expression via target mRNA cleavage, translational repression, and mediation of DNA methylation. miRNAs target transcription factors and hormone signaling pathways to regulate cotton plant architecture and fiber development. In addition, miRNAs mitigate biotic and abiotic stresses through ROS, lignin, and hormone pathways, as well as by forming competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) modules with long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs). This review establishes an miRNA-centered regulatory framework that coordinates cotton growth, development, and stress resistance. A series of technologies, including multi-omics combined with machine learning, gene overexpression, STTM, MIM, MIGS, CRISPR editing, foliar dsRNA spraying, and bionanocarriers, are proposed to facilitate the breeding of cotton varieties with high yield, superior fiber quality, and broad-spectrum stress tolerance.

title: MicroRNA Gatekeepers: Integrating Growth, Development, and Stress Adaptation in Cotton.

abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) severely limited drug delivery into the brain, while aberrant aerobic glycolysis in the tumor microenvironment caused excessive lactate accumulation and drove immunosuppression. These factors together constituted the core obstacles to glioblastoma (GBM) therapy. From the perspective of metabolism-immune crosstalk, we engineered a brain‑targeted nucleic acid nanosphere (TE@siP‑DNS/DOX) featuring high BBB/BBTB penetrability, which orchestrated a "triple‑linked" strategy integrating glycolysis blockade, immune microenvironment remodeling, and synergistic therapeutic potentiation. The nanosphere was constructed with a self‑assembled core of PKM2‑targeting siRNA and framework nucleic acids loaded with doxorubicin (DOX), shielded by a biomimetic shell of T7 peptide‑modified macrophage extracellular vesicles. Leveraging transcytosis and T7‑mediated active targeting, TE@siP‑DNS/DOX efficiently traversed the barriers and preferentially accumulated at tumor sites. DOX simultaneously provoked chemotherapy and immunogenic cell death, igniting robust CD8⁺ T cell‑mediated antitumor immunity, whereas siRNA‑mediated PKM2 silencing curtailed glycolysis, lessened lactate production, rewired metabolic circuitry, and forced macrophage polarization toward the M1 antitumor phenotype, thereby dismantling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (iTME). Transcriptomic analysis further confirmed that metabolic and immune-related pathways were significantly enriched following TE@siP-DNS/DOX treatment, providing transcriptional evidence for its dual modulation of the metabolic-immune feedback loop. In vivo studies substantiated that TE@siP‑DNS/DOX markedly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic GBM-bearing mice. Collectively, this nanoplatform, through a synergistic feedback loop integrating metabolic regulation and immune activation, provides a good therapeutic strategy and research paradigm for enhanced glioma therapy. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Glioblastoma therapy is impeded by a multifaceted barrier system encompassing the blood-brain barrier, metabolic dysregulation, lactate accumulation, and immunosuppression. Here, we engineered a brain-targeted nucleic acid nanosphere that integrates glycolysis blockade, immune remodeling, and chemotherapeutic sensitization via a single platform. By combining PKM2 silencing with doxorubicin-loaded framework nucleic acids and T7-modified macrophage vesicles, the nanosphere achieves efficient barrier penetration, lactate reduction, M1 macrophage repolarization, and immunogenic cell death. This metabolism-immune feedback loop synergistically suppresses orthotopic tumors and extends survival. Our study provides a paradigm for treating brain tumors through concurrent metabolic reprogramming and antitumor immunity, offering a translatable strategy for overcoming therapy resistance in glioblastoma.

title: Macrophage Extracellular Vesicle-Camouflaged Framework Nucleic Acid Nanospheres Reprogram Lactate Metabolism-Immune Feedback Loops for Synergistic Chemoimmunotherapy of Glioblastoma.

abstract: Lung cancer is the most common type of cancer worldwide. Tumors carrying a mutation in the STK11 gene are associated with severe prognosis and resistance to therapy. New treatments for pulmonary adenocarcinoma highlight the efficacy of High-LET neutron therapy, often combined with drug therapy. PCSK9, whose inhibitors are used to treat dyslipidemia, may also be a new target in lung cancer therapy. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated STK11 mutation was performed in murine LLC1 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Human A549 cells that naturally carry a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the STK11 gene were also used. Cells were irradiated with protons, neutrons, and photons (2 Gy) and analyzed for survival, apoptosis, clonogenic survival assay, and evolocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor) sensitivity. In vivo xenograft (Nude) and syngeneic (C57BL/6) subcutaneous tumor models were neutron-irradiated (5 Gy). Tumor cell proliferation, microenvironment, and protein expression were assessed. High-LET irradiation confirmed the STK11-deficient lines radio resistance, which did not reduce under PCSK9 inhibitor treatment conditions in vitro. In animal models, the PCSK9 inhibitor decreased Ki67 index of tumor cells and infiltration of cancer-associated fibroblasts and macrophages in the combination therapy group. Particle therapy resistance serves as a crucial prognostic marker in the management of lung adenocarcinoma. Using cell lines and animal models, we successfully described this resistance phenotype and demonstrated the promising use of a PCSK9 inhibitor to enhance the efficacy of hadron radiotherapy against lung cancer.

title: Combined Effect of Hadron Therapy and PCSK9 Inhibition Therapy on the Immune Response in STK11-Deficient Lung Adenocarcinoma.

abstract: Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal sphingolipidosis caused by the deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (GALC), leading to profound alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and severe neurodegeneration. While psychosine (Psy) accumulation is a well-established hallmark of KD, emerging evidence suggests that lactosylceramide (LacCer) may also contribute to disease pathogenesis. Here, we generated a novel human oligodendrocytic model of GALC deficiency by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated GALC knockout in MO3.13 cells and used it to investigate sphingolipid alterations associated with impaired GALC activity. GALC-/- MO3.13 cells showed a marked reduction in GALC transcript levels and enzymatic activity, confirming the successful establishment of a disease-relevant cellular model. Our results demonstrated that a) GALC knockout MO3.13 cells accumulated Psy and LacCer, and b) LacCer content was increased in the brain and heart isolated from twitcher (TWI) mice, the most widely used spontaneous animal model of KD. In parallel, AKT signalling was evaluated in both systems, supporting a link between LacCer dysregulation and altered cellular signalling pathways. Overall, these findings identify LacCer accumulation as a conserved feature of GALC deficiency across cellular and animal models and support the use of GALC-/- MO3.13 cells as a novel in vitro platform to investigate KD pathogenesis and candidate therapeutic strategies.

title: A new CRISPR/Cas9 GALC Knockout Cellular Model Reveals Lactosylceramide Accumulation Similar to Twitcher Mice.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Bone metastasis (BM) occurs in approximately 70% of patients with advanced breast cancer (BCa) and is associated with limited treatment options and a median survival of only 19-25 months. Although microtubule (MT)-targeting agents such as paclitaxel remain a standard therapy, their efficacy is often limited by chemoresistance linked to in part by altered β-tubulin isotype expression. Among these, tubulin β2a and tubulin β3 (encoded by TUBB2A and TUBB3) have been linked to poor clinical outcomes; however, their roles in breast cancer bone metastasis (BMBC) remain unclear. Here, we investigated the functional significance of TUBB2A and TUBB3 in regulating MT dynamics and metastatic behavior in bone-derived BCa cells. Methods: TUBB2A and TUBB3 expression levels were evaluated in primary breast tumors and bone metastases. CRISPR-mediated TUBB2A knockout and TUBB3 depletion were performed in bone-derived MDA-MB-231 cells to assess microtubule dynamics, trafficking, metastatic phenotypes, and gene expression. Results: Elevated expression of both TUBB2A and TUBB3 correlated with reduced patient survival. Immunohistochemical analyses demonstrated increased tubulin β2a abundance in BM lesions relative to matched primary breast tumors, while the proportion of moderate-to-strong tubulin-β3-positive cells was also increased in BM. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout/knockdown in a bone-derived MDA-MB-231 cell model, we found that loss of TUBB2A or partial depletion of TUBB3 impaired MT regrowth, altered the cell cycle, and disrupted endosomal trafficking, characterized by enlarged perinuclear Rab5-positive vesicles. Functionally, depletion of either isotype reduced cell migration and invasion while enhancing adhesion, accompanied by increased expression of integrin β4, β5, α4, α5, and talin-1. Exploratory RNA-seq analysis suggests enrichment of cytokine-cytokine receptor signaling pathways, consistent with a potential link between MT remodeling and inflammatory/secretory programs. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings identify TUBB2A and TUBB3 as regulators of metastatic phenotypes and potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in BMBC.

title: A Novel Function of Tubulin β2a and Tubulin β3 in Regulating Metastatic Properties in Bone-Metastatic Breast Cancer Cells.

abstract: Cystic fibrosis is a life-threatening inherited disease caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene that impair chloride and bicarbonate transport across airway epithelia. Gene editing and cell replacement strategies hold promise for restoring CFTR function, yet they inevitably generate heterogeneous cell populations in which only a fraction of cells carry a corrected allele, raising the question of how large this fraction must be for functional rescue to be detectable and whether the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assay is sensitive enough to capture partial correction. To address this, we generated chimeric iPSC-derived lung organoids by co-culturing GFP-labeled wild-type airway basal cells with unlabeled F508del-homozygous cystic fibrosis basal cells at seven predefined ratios (0-100% wild-type), verifying the actual wild-type fraction by flow cytometry and quantifying 24-h forskolin-induced swelling as the area ratio. Chimeric organoids showed a dose-dependent increase in swelling with rising wild-type fractions, with a statistically significant FIS response first resolved at approximately 6% wild-type cells in the pooled analysis. Separately, ROC analysis of well-level data identified two area-ratio cutoffs for classifying organoid populations-1.16 (80% sensitivity, 80% specificity) and 1.21 (98% specificity, 70% sensitivity)-which the fitted mean response reaches at approximately 14% and 34% wild-type cells, respectively. The minimum statistically detectable fraction and the classification cutoffs are distinct quantities derived from different analyses and are not interchangeable; both describe the performance of the FIS assay in heterogeneous organoids rather than thresholds for therapeutic benefit and provide a practical reference framework for designing and interpreting gene editing and cell therapy studies in cystic fibrosis.

title: Chimeric iPSC-Derived Lung Organoids Reveal the Minimum Wild-Type Cell Fraction Detectable by the Forskolin-Induced Swelling Assay in Cystic Fibrosis.

abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

title: Temporal proteomics maps concealed-stage remodeling and reveals early mitochondrial alteration as an intervention target in a model of PKP2-arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

abstract: Synonymous evolution can alter both codon abundance and the placement of synonymous codons within genes. We asked whether plastid coding sequences retain non-random codon-boundary organization after protein sequence and exact codon inventory are held constant. We analysed 44 genes lacking an RNA-editing exception flag in the reference annotation across 18 Platycerium species, using exact-codon conditional randomization as the principal analysis and RSCU comparisons as supporting phylogenetic context. CpG boundaries were depleted across species and most genes, with the direction retained under reconstruction and gene-length sensitivities. TpA showed greater gene-level heterogeneity. Both patterns belonged to a coupled landscape of 16 boundary contexts, in which GpT had the lowest observed/expected ratio. These observations distinguish synonymous placement from codon abundance without identifying the evolutionary processes responsible. Shared ancestry, context-dependent mutation, and local sequence constraints remain compatible explanations. The results establish a boundary-order pattern within the sampled matrix and motivate phylogenetically informed comparisons to distinguish historical retention from continued maintenance or recurrent change.

title: Conditional Codon-Boundary Dinucleotide Organization in Platycerium Plastomes.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Mitophagy, the selective clearance of defective mitochondria via the autophagy-lysosome pathway, is essential for maintaining mitochondrial health and cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation of mitophagy is strongly implicated in aging-related pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and metabolic disorders, highlighting the significance of elucidating its regulatory mechanisms. While existing methods using exogenous reporters enable genome-wide and high-throughput screening for mitophagy regulators, they constrain discoveries to specific pathways and introduce artifacts through ectopic expression.
OBJECTIVES: To overcome these limitations, we developed an effective and rapid platform for identifying mitophagy modulators by targeting endogenous proteins.
METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we engineered HeLa cells expressing small molecular tags (GFP or NanoLuc) fused to the C-terminal of ATP5B, a mitochondrial inner membrane protein. Genome-wide screening for mitophagy regulatory genes were performed using a genome-wide CRISPR library coupled with flow cytometry. Additionally, an FDA-approved kinase inhibitor library was used to screen for mitophagy inducers. To evaluate the efficacy of a screened drug in Alzheimer's disease, cognitive behavior, pathological features and mitophagy events in 3 × Tg-AD mice with or without treatment were examined using the Morris water maze assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
RESULTS: These ATP5B-tagging cells provided a robust readout of mitophagy and enabled high-throughput genetic or pharmacological screening. With this platform, we identified several promising genes that regulate mitophagy and are significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, the FDA-approved drug Flupentixol emerged as a novel mitophagy inducer that acts by promoting adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) localization to mitochondria and exhibited strong therapeutic potential in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
CONCLUSION: This study establishes a novel system for identifying mitophagy modulators, with the potential to accelerate the discovery of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.

abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.
